paragraphs.text: Honey is a substance produced by bees from the sweet liquid called nectar that is found in flowers. Its composition and colour depend on the type of flower that supplies the nectar; for example clover flowers produce a white honey, while the fragrant plant lavender produces a deeper orange-yellow. Although many types of bees produce honey, the honeybee is the most productive and is the one most commonly associated with honey harvesting. Inside their nests, bees create a structure known as honeycomb, or simply 'comb', consisting of small hexagonal cells, where eggs, young bees and honey are stored. It is this comb that beekeepers collect when harvesting honey.

Bees live together in groups known as colonies. An average colony produces 27-45kg of honey each year. There are three types of bees in a colony:50,000-70,000 workers, which are all female, one queen, and 2,000 males. When worker bees are about 20 days old, they leave the nest to collect nectar. They suck the nectar from the flower with their tongues and deposit it into their abdomens. As the nectar journeys through the bee's body, water is drawn out, and the bee's glandular system produces enzymes that make the nectar more nutritious. When worker bees cannot hold any more nectar, they return to the nest. The processed nectar, now on its way to becoming honey, is put into empty honeycomb cells. Other worker bees eat the honey, repeating the process. When the honey has fully matured, it is deposited into a honeycomb cell one last time and sealed with wax.

Honey has always been held in high regard. In ancient times, it was considered a symbol of wealth in addition to being a food source, and in the Middle Ages it was the basis for the production of a widely consumed beverage called mead. There are records of early beekeeping in various parts of the world, including Ancient Egypt, Greece and China. Some early beekeepers created artificial nests for colonies, known as hives, in cylinders made of bark, reed, straw, mud or clay. The bees then made their combs inside the cylinders. However, the process of extracting the comb resulted in its destruction, which in turn led to the destruction of the colony. Over the years, beekeepers came up with various ingenious solutions to this problem. One such invention was the 'skep'. This was essentially a basket placed upside-down over the hive, and the full combs were removed from underneath. A further innovation called for cutting a hole in the top of the hive and placing a straw or wooden box over the hole. This box would eventually fill with honey as well, and it could then be removed without harming the comb.

Honeybees were first taken to North America in the mid-1600s, probably by settlers who travelled from England in the early 1620s. Although there were already bees on the North American continent, they were a different species to honeybees. Once introduced, honeybees were able to increase their range by moving to new territories. The early settlers noticed they preferred hollow logs, and so started placing sticks crosswise over the opening of the logs to support the honeycombs. This not only allowed for the comb to be removed from one end, but also kept the comb intact so that the colony could use it again.

In the mid-nineteenth century in Green County, New York, a woodworker and keen beekeeper, Moses Quinby, improved upon the beekeeping system of the time by layering a number of boxes over the main chamber. Meanwhile, another beekeeper of the period, Lorenzo Langstroth of Philadelphia, invented a hive with moveable frames which allowed for easy extraction and reinsertion of the combs. This design is the basis for the hives which are still in use today, as part of an industry currently producing 1.8 million tonnes of honey per year.

Modern-day honey production also includes the manufacture of a range of goods related to the finished honey. These are obtained from various stages of the production process from hive to jar. The most common products are beeswax, pollen, royal jelly, and propolis. Beeswax is produced as the nectar is transforming into honey inside the bee, with the wax being expelled through glands in its body. The colony collects the wax to cover the filled honeycomb cells. It is scraped off by the beekeeper and can be sold to manufacturers for use in the production of items like cosmetics and candles. Pollen sticks on the legs of the worker bees as they collect flower nectar. Because pollen contains large amounts of vitamin B12 and vitamin E, and has more protein than beef, it is highly nutritious and used as a dietary supplement. Royal jelly is a creamy liquid produced to feed the queen. Nutrient-rich, it is highly valued for use in skin creams, lotions and oils, and is also sold as a dietary supplement. Many believe it increases energy, and helps to reduce anxiety, sleeplessness, and memory loss.

Propolis is plant resin, collected from the buds of plants, combined with bee saliva and beeswax. This is used to cover cracks in the hive, and to reduce the size of the hive opening during the winter. Propolis is used commercially as a disinfectant, as well as in the treatment of problems such as gum disease and respiratory illnesses. It can even be used as an ingredient for varnish to protect violins and cellos.

questions.prompt: Bees that consume lavender produce more strongly flavoured honey.
There are certain species of bees which can make greater quantities of honey than the honeybee.
Nectar is collected by the female bees in a colony.
People in the Middle Ages made a popular drink produced from honey.
Production of honey using a skep involved destroying the colony.
The bees imported into North America produced a higher quality of honey than the native species.
Early settlers in North America put sticks over the entrance of hollow logs to prevent combs being destroyed.
